name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q01 - Opposing factors determining stability of solid state

questiontext.text: Under a given set of conditions of temperature and pressure, the stability of the solid state of a substance is governed by the net effect of which two opposing factors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Matter exists in solid, liquid, or gaseous states depending on the balance between attractive forces and particle motion.

Step 2: Evaluation
Intermolecular forces tend to bring constituent particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) closer together, whereas thermal energy tends to keep them apart by making them move faster. At sufficiently low temperatures, thermal energy is low and intermolecular forces hold the particles in fixed positions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two opposing factors determining the stability of a state are intermolecular forces and thermal energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q02 - Reason for rigidity in solids

questiontext.text: Solids are rigid and incompressible primarily because their constituent particles:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unlike fluids (liquids and gases) whose molecules are free to move about, solids maintain a definite shape and volume.

Step 2: Evaluation
In solids, intermolecular distances are short and intermolecular forces are strong. Consequently, the constituent particles occupy fixed positions and can only oscillate about their mean positions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Rigidity in solids arises because their constituent particles have fixed positions and can only oscillate about their mean positions.

answer.text: undergo rapid translational motion throughout the bulk
have fixed positions and can only oscillate about their mean positions
are separated by very large intermolecular distances

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q05 - Why ancient glass objects appear milky

Ancient glass appears milky due to partial crystallisation over time.

Anisotropy means that physical properties such as electrical resistance or refractive index have different values when measured along different directions in the same crystal.

In a crystal, the constituent particles are arranged in an ordered, periodic manner such that the arrangement and spacing of particles differ along different crystallographic directions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Anisotropy in crystals arises from the different arrangement of constituent particles along different directions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q07 - Cleavage and refractive index of amorphous solid

questiontext.text: The refractive index of a solid is observed to have the same value along all directions. Which of the following statements is true about this solid?

A solid whose physical properties such as refractive index are identical in all directions is isotropic, which is a hallmark of amorphous solids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Amorphous solids have only short-range order and behave like supercooled liquids. When cut with a sharp-edged tool, they break into two pieces with irregular surfaces rather than showing clean cleavage into plain, smooth surfaces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The solid is amorphous and does not show clean cleavage with smooth surfaces.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q08 - Polycrystalline metals appearing isotropic

questiontext.text: Why does a bulk metallic sample often appear isotropic even though a single crystal of the metal is anisotropic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Metals commonly exist in a polycrystalline state consisting of numerous tiny microcrystals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although each individual microcrystal is anisotropic, the microcrystals in a polycrystalline sample are randomly oriented in all directions, averaging out directional differences in physical properties.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A bulk metallic sample appears isotropic because it is polycrystalline with randomly oriented microcrystals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q09 - Converting quartz into quartz glass

questiontext.text: Under what conditions can crystalline quartz be converted into amorphous quartz glass?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quartz is a crystalline form of \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) with long-range order, whereas quartz glass is its amorphous form with only short-range order.

Step 2: Evaluation
Melting quartz breaks its long-range crystalline order. If the molten silica is then cooled rapidly, the particles do not have enough time to arrange into a regular repeating crystal lattice, freezing into an amorphous glass.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Quartz can be converted into glass by melting it and then cooling the melt rapidly.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q10 - Classification of solid SO2 and NH3

questiontext.text: Solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) and solid \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) are examples of which type of crystalline solids?

Molecular solids are subdivided into non-polar, polar, and hydrogen-bonded molecular solids depending on the intermolecular forces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) and solid \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) are examples of polar molecular solids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q11 - Classification of P4O10 and (NH4)3PO4

questiontext.text: Tetra phosphorus decoxide (\(\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{10}\)) and ammonium phosphate (\((\mathrm{NH}_4)_3\mathrm{PO}_4\)) are classified respectively as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Crystalline solids are classified based on the constituent particles and the binding forces between them.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{10}\) consists of discrete covalent molecules held together by intermolecular forces, making it a molecular solid. \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) consists of \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) cations and \(\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\) anions bound by electrostatic forces, making it an ionic solid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{10}\) is a molecular solid and \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) is an ionic solid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q12 - Electrical conductivity of ionic solids

questiontext.text: Ionic solids are electrical insulators in the solid state, but conduct electricity in the molten state or in aqueous solution because:

generalfeedback.text:

Electrical conduction requires mobile charge carriers such as free electrons or free ions.

Step 2: Evaluation
In solid ionic crystals, cations and anions are held in fixed positions by strong coulombic forces and cannot move freely. Upon melting or dissolving in water, the rigid lattice breaks down and the ions become free to move and carry electric current.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ions are fixed in the solid state, whereas they become free to move in the molten state or aqueous solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q13 - Identifying covalent network solid from properties

questiontext.text: A solid X is very hard, acts as an electrical insulator in both the solid and molten states, and melts at an extremely high temperature. Solid X is a:

generalfeedback.text:

Crystalline solids differ in hardness, melting point, and electrical conductivity in solid and molten states.

Ionic solids conduct electricity in the molten state, metallic solids conduct in both solid and molten states, and molecular solids have low melting points. Only covalent (network) solids such as diamond, \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\), and \(\mathrm{SiC}\) are very hard, have extremely high melting points, and remain electrical insulators in both solid and molten states.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Solid X is a covalent (network) solid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q14 - Exceptional conductivity and softness of graphite

questiontext.text: Although graphite is a covalent solid, it is soft and a good conductor of electricity because:

In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three neighbours in the same layer, leaving the fourth valence electron free to move between layers, which accounts for electrical conductivity. Moreover, weak forces between layers allow them to slide over one another, making graphite soft.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Graphite is soft and conductive because its layers can slide over one another and each carbon atom has a free fourth valence electron.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q15 - Classification of brass, Rb, LiBr, and Si

Metals and alloys (like \(\mathrm{Rb}\) and brass) are metallic solids, whereas non-metals or metalloids forming extended covalent networks (like \(\mathrm{Si}\), \(\mathrm{SiC}\), and graphite) are covalent solids.

Rubidium (\(\mathrm{Rb}\)) and brass are metallic solids. Silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)) and \(\mathrm{SiC}\) are covalent network solids. \(\mathrm{LiBr}\) is an ionic solid, while \(\mathrm{I}_2\) and \(\mathrm{P}_4\) are molecular solids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q16 - Reason for brittleness of ionic solids

questiontext.text: Ionic solids are hard and brittle because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionic crystals consist of alternating cations and anions held by strong, non-directional electrostatic forces.

Step 2: Evaluation
The strong coulombic attractions make ionic solids hard. However, when a shearing force is applied, layers of ions shift slightly, bringing ions of like charge adjacent to one another. The resulting electrostatic repulsion causes the crystal to cleave or shatter, making it brittle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ionic solids are hard due to strong electrostatic forces and brittle because shearing brings like-charged ions adjacent to each other, causing repulsion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q17 - Parameters characterising a 3D unit cell

questiontext.text: How many parameters characterise a three-dimensional unit cell, and what are they?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A three-dimensional unit cell is a parallelepiped defined by its edge lengths and the angles between those edges.

Step 2: Evaluation
It is characterised by six parameters: three edge lengths \(a, b, c\) and three interaxial angles \(\alpha\) (between \(b\) and \(c\)), \(\beta\) (between \(a\) and \(c\)), and \(\gamma\) (between \(a\) and \(b\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Six parameters (\(a, b, c, \alpha, \beta, \gamma\)) characterise a three-dimensional unit cell.

answer.text: Eight: four edge lengths and four angles

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q18 - Total number of Bravais lattices

questiontext.text: What is the total number of possible three-dimensional Bravais lattices across all seven crystal systems?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Combining the seven primitive crystal systems with possible centred unit cells (body-centred, face-centred, and end-centred) yields the Bravais lattices.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bravais demonstrated that there are exactly \(14\) possible three-dimensional space lattices: \(3\) cubic, \(2\) tetragonal, \(4\) orthorhombic, \(1\) hexagonal, \(1\) rhombohedral, \(2\) monoclinic, and \(1\) triclinic (\(3 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 14\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are \(14\) possible three-dimensional Bravais lattices.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q19 - Crystal system with all four Bravais lattice types

questiontext.text: Which crystal system exhibits all four types of unit cells: primitive, body-centred, face-centred, and end-centred?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Among the seven crystal systems, only one accommodates all four Bravais lattice variations.

Step 2: Evaluation
The orthorhombic crystal system (\(a \neq b \neq c\), \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ\)) has primitive, body-centred, face-centred, and end-centred unit cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The orthorhombic crystal system exhibits all four unit cell variations.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q20 - Distinguishing hexagonal and monoclinic unit cells

questiontext.text: Which set of axial parameters correctly represents a monoclinic unit cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each of the seven crystal systems has a distinct combination of edge-length relationships and interaxial angles.

Step 2: Evaluation
A monoclinic unit cell has three unequal edge lengths (\(a eq b eq c\)), two angles equal to \(90^\circ\) (\(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ\)), and one angle different from \(90^\circ\) (\( eta eq 90^\circ\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The monoclinic unit cell is defined by \(a eq b eq c\) and \(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ,\ eta eq 90^\circ\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q21 - Difference between face centred and end centred unit cell

questiontext.text: How does a face-centred unit cell differ from an end-centred unit cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both face-centred and end-centred unit cells are centred unit cells with particles at all corners plus additional particles at face centres.

Step 2: Evaluation
A face-centred unit cell has one constituent particle at the centre of each of the six faces in addition to the corners. An end-centred unit cell has one constituent particle at the centre of only two opposite faces in addition to the corners.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A face-centred unit cell has particles at the centres of all six faces, whereas an end-centred unit cell has particles at the centres of only two opposite faces.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q23 - Lattice points in face centred tetragonal and bcc unit cells

questiontext.text: How many lattice points are present in one unit cell of (i) face-centred cubic and (ii) body-centred cubic lattices, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of lattice points in a unit cell equals the total number of corner and centred positions (note: lattice points are the geometric sites in one unit cell, counted as \(8\) corners + \(6\) face centres = \(14\) for fcc, and \(8\) corners + \(1\) body centre = \(9\) for bcc, whereas effective atoms per unit cell are \(4\) and \(2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
In a face-centred cubic unit cell, there are \(8\) corner lattice points and \(6\) face-centred lattice points, giving \(8 + 6 = 14\) lattice points. In a body-centred cubic unit cell, there are \(8\) corner lattice points and \(1\) body-centred lattice point, giving \(8 + 1 = 9\) lattice points.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are \(14\) lattice points in a face-centred cubic unit cell and \(9\) lattice points in a body-centred cubic unit cell.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q24 - Fraction of corner atom in cubic unit cell

questiontext.text: What portion of an atom located at the corner of a cubic unit cell belongs to that particular unit cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a three-dimensional cubic lattice, each corner is shared equally by adjacent unit cells meeting at that point.

Step 2: Evaluation
A corner atom is shared between \(8\) adjacent unit cells (\(4\) in the same layer and \(4\) in the upper or lower layer). Therefore, \(\frac{1}{8}\) of the corner atom belongs to one particular unit cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\frac{1}{8}\) of a corner atom belongs to a particular cubic unit cell.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q25 - Total number of atoms in bcc and fcc unit cells

questiontext.text: The total number of atoms per unit cell in a body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice and a face-centred cubic (fcc) lattice are, respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We consider a bcc unit cell and an fcc unit cell.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each corner atom contributes \(\frac{1}{8}\), each face-centre atom contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\), and a body-centre atom contributes \(1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(z = \sum (\text{number of sites} \times \text{fractional contribution})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For bcc: \(z = 8 \times \frac{1}{8} + 1 \times 1 = 1 + 1 = 2\) atoms.
For fcc: \(z = 8 \times \frac{1}{8} + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1 + 3 = 4\) atoms.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The effective numbers of atoms per unit cell are \(2\) for bcc and \(4\) for fcc.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q26 - Formula and coordination numbers of cubic solid PQ

questiontext.text: A cubic solid is made of two elements \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\). Atoms of \(\mathrm{Q}\) are at the corners of the cube and \(\mathrm{P}\) is at the body-centre. What is the formula of the compound and what are the coordination numbers of \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\mathrm{Q}\) atoms occupy the \(8\) corners of the cube, and \(\mathrm{P}\) occupies the body-centre.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Corner contribution is \(\frac{1}{8}\) per unit cell and body-centre contribution is \(1\) per unit cell.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Formula is determined by the ratio of effective atoms of \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\) in one unit cell.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of \(\mathrm{Q}\) atoms per unit cell \(= 8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1\).
Number of \(\mathrm{P}\) atoms per unit cell \(= 1 \times 1 = 1\).
Ratio \(\mathrm{P}:\mathrm{Q} = 1:1 \implies \mathrm{PQ}\).
The body-centred atom \(\mathrm{P}\) is surrounded by \(8\) corner \(\mathrm{Q}\) atoms, so its coordination number is \(8\). By symmetry in the \(\mathrm{CsCl}\)-type lattice, each corner \(\mathrm{Q}\) atom is shared by \(8\) cubes and is surrounded by \(8\) body-centred \(\mathrm{P}\) atoms, so its coordination number is also \(8\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The formula is \(\mathrm{PQ}\), and the coordination numbers of both \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\) are \(8\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q27 - Formula of cubic crystal with missing corner atom

questiontext.text: In a face-centred cubic unit cell of a compound formed by elements \(\mathrm{X}\) and \(\mathrm{Y}\), atoms of \(\mathrm{X}\) occupy all corners except one corner which is vacant, and atoms of \(\mathrm{Y}\) occupy all the face centres. What is the simplest formula of the compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Out of \(8\) corners, \(7\) are occupied by \(\mathrm{X}\) atoms. All \(6\) face centres are occupied by \(\mathrm{Y}\) atoms.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each corner atom contributes \(\frac{1}{8}\) and each face-centre atom contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\) to the unit cell.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Effective atoms per unit cell determine the stoichiometric ratio \(\mathrm{X}:\mathrm{Y}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of \(\mathrm{X}\) atoms per unit cell \(= 7 \times \frac{1}{8} = \frac{7}{8}\).
Number of \(\mathrm{Y}\) atoms per unit cell \(= 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\).
Ratio \(\mathrm{X}:\mathrm{Y} = \frac{7}{8} : 3 = 7 : 24\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(7\) and \(24\) have no common factor other than \(1\), so the simplest formula is \(\mathrm{X}_7\mathrm{Y}_{24}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q28 - Two dimensional coordination number in square close packing

questiontext.text: What is the two-dimensional coordination number of a sphere in a square close-packed layer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coordination number is the number of nearest-neighbour spheres in direct contact with a given sphere.

Step 2: Evaluation
In two-dimensional square close packing (\(\text{AAA}\) type), each sphere is in contact with \(4\) immediate neighbouring spheres whose centres form a square.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two-dimensional coordination number in square close packing is \(4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q29 - Stacking pattern in hcp and ccp structures

questiontext.text: Which stacking pattern of two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layers gives a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure, and which gives a cubic close-packed (ccp) structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Placing a third layer over the second layer either covers tetrahedral voids (repeating the first layer) or covers octahedral voids (forming a new third orientation).

Step 2: Evaluation
Covering tetrahedral voids aligns the third layer with the first, producing an \(\text{ABAB}\ldots\) pattern called hexagonal close packing (hcp). Covering octahedral voids places the third layer in a new orientation C, aligning the fourth layer with the first, producing an \(\text{ABCABC}\ldots\) pattern called cubic close packing (ccp).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
hcp has the \(\text{ABAB}\ldots\) pattern and ccp has the \(\text{ABCABC}\ldots\) pattern.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q30 - Total voids and tetrahedral voids in 0.5 mol hcp

questiontext.text: A compound forms a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. What is the total number of voids in \(0.5\text{ mol}\) of it, and how many of these are tetrahedral voids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amount of close-packed atoms \(= 0.5\text{ mol}\); Avogadro constant \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For \(N\) close-packed spheres, there are \(N\) octahedral voids and \(2N\) tetrahedral voids, giving \(3N\) total voids.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(N = n \times N_A\); tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); total voids \(= 3N\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of close-packed atoms \(N = 0.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{23}\).
Number of octahedral voids \(= 3.011 \times 10^{23}\).
Number of tetrahedral voids \(= 2 \times 3.011 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\).
Total number of voids \(= 3.011 \times 10^{23} + 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 9.033 \times 10^{23}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total voids are \(9.033 \times 10^{23}\) and tetrahedral voids are \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q31 - Formula of compound with 1/3 tetrahedral voids occupied

questiontext.text: A compound is formed by two elements \(\mathrm{M}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\). Element \(\mathrm{N}\) forms a ccp lattice and atoms of \(\mathrm{M}\) occupy \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the tetrahedral voids. What is the formula of the compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Element \(\mathrm{N}\) forms a ccp lattice; \(\mathrm{M}\) occupies \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the tetrahedral voids.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the number of \(\mathrm{N}\) atoms in the ccp lattice be \(N_0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of tetrahedral voids \(= 2N_0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of \(\mathrm{M}\) atoms \(= \frac{1}{3} \times 2N_0 = \frac{2}{3}N_0\).
Ratio \(\mathrm{M}:\mathrm{N} = \frac{2}{3} : 1 = 2 : 3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The simplest whole-number formula of the compound is \(\mathrm{M}_2\mathrm{N}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q32 - Formula of ferric oxide from hcp and octahedral holes

questiontext.text: Ferric oxide crystallises in a hexagonal close-packed array of oxide ions with two out of every three octahedral holes occupied by ferric ions. What is the formula of ferric oxide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Oxide ions (\(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\)) form an hcp array; ferric ions (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)) occupy \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the octahedral voids.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the number of oxide ions in the hcp array be \(N\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of octahedral voids equals \(N\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions \(= \frac{2}{3}N\).
Ratio \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} : \mathrm{O}^{2-} = \frac{2}{3} : 1 = 2 : 3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Charge neutrality check: \(2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0\). The formula of ferric oxide is \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q33 - Coordination number in ccp and bcc

questiontext.text: What is the coordination number of atoms in (i) a cubic close-packed (ccp) structure and (ii) a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coordination number is the number of nearest neighbours in direct contact with an atom in the crystal.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a cubic close-packed (ccp/fcc) structure, each atom touches \(6\) atoms in its own layer, \(3\) in the layer above, and \(3\) in the layer below, giving a coordination number of \(12\). In a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure, the body-centre atom touches \(8\) corner atoms, giving a coordination number of \(8\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The coordination numbers are \(12\) in ccp and \(8\) in bcc.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q34 - Location of octahedral voids in fcc unit cell

questiontext.text: In a face-centred cubic (ccp) unit cell, where are the \(4\) octahedral voids effectively located?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An octahedral void is surrounded by six close-packed spheres at the vertices of a regular octahedron.

Step 2: Evaluation
In an fcc unit cell, there is \(1\) octahedral void at the body centre (surrounded by \(6\) face-centred atoms, contributing \(1\)) and \(1\) octahedral void at the centre of each of the \(12\) edges (each shared by \(4\) unit cells, contributing \(12 \times \frac{1}{4} = 3\)). Total octahedral voids \(= 1 + 3 = 4\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(4\) octahedral voids are located at the body centre (\(1\)) and at the centres of the \(12\) edges (\(12 \times \frac{1}{4} = 3\)).

answer.text: All \(4\) inside the \(8\) small octants of the cube
\(1\) at the body centre and \(1\) at the centre of each of the \(12\) edges
\(1\) at each of the \(6\) face centres and \(1\) at the body centre
\(8\) at the corners and \(6\) at the face centres

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q35 - Relation between octahedral void radius r and sphere radius R

questiontext.text: If \(r\) is the radius of an octahedral void and \(R\) is the radius of the spheres in close packing, what is the relation between \(r\) and \(R\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An octahedral void of radius \(r\) sits at the centre of an octahedron formed by six close-packed spheres of radius \(R\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the equatorial square plane of the octahedron, four spheres of radius \(R\) touch each other along the sides of a square of side \(2R\), and the void sphere of radius \(r\) touches all four along the diagonal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In a right-angled triangle formed by two adjacent sides of the square and its diagonal, \(\text{diagonal}^2 = (2R)^2 + (2R)^2\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The diagonal length is \(2R + 2r = \sqrt{(2R)^2 + (2R)^2} = 2\sqrt{2}R\).
Dividing both sides by \(2\):
\[R + r = \sqrt{2}R \implies r = (\sqrt{2} - 1)R \approx (1.414 - 1)R = 0.414R\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(0.414R < R\), the void is smaller than the host spheres. Thus, \(r = 0.414R\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q36 - Locating tetrahedral voids in ccp unit cell

questiontext.text: When a ccp (fcc) unit cell is divided into \(8\) equal small cubes (octants), how many tetrahedral voids are present in each small cube and how are the \(4\) surrounding atoms arranged on each small cube?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A ccp unit cell contains \(4\) atoms and therefore \(2 \times 4 = 8\) tetrahedral voids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Dividing the ccp cube into \(8\) small cubes gives one small cube per tetrahedral void. Each small cube has atoms at \(4\) alternate corners, which form a regular tetrahedron enclosing \(1\) tetrahedral void at the centre of that small cube.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There is \(1\) tetrahedral void in each small cube, surrounded by \(4\) atoms at alternate corners of the small cube.

answer.text: \(2\) tetrahedral voids per small cube; atoms at all \(8\) corners
\(1\) tetrahedral void per small cube; atoms at \(4\) alternate corners
\(1\) tetrahedral void per small cube; atoms at \(4\) adjacent corners on one face
\(4\) tetrahedral voids per small cube; atoms at \(4\) alternate corners

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q37 - Lattice with highest packing efficiency

questiontext.text: Which of the following lattices has the highest packing efficiency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Packing efficiency is the percentage of total unit cell space occupied by constituent spheres.

Step 2: Evaluation
Simple cubic lattice has \(52.4\%\) packing efficiency, body-centred cubic (bcc) has \(68\%\), and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and cubic close-packed (ccp/fcc) lattices have \(74\%\) packing efficiency.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice has the highest packing efficiency (\(74\%\)) among the given options.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q38 - Percentage of empty space in bcc lattice

questiontext.text: What percentage of total space is vacant (unoccupied) in a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We consider a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Total space in the unit cell is \(100\%\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Vacant space (\%)} = 100\% - \text{Packing efficiency (\%)} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The packing efficiency of a bcc unit cell is \(68\%\).
Therefore, vacant space \(= 100\% - 68\% = 32\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(68\% + 32\% = 100\%\). Thus, \(32\%\) of the space is vacant in a bcc unit cell.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q39 - Edge length of gold fcc unit cell

questiontext.text: Gold (atomic radius \(= 0.144\text{ nm}\)) crystallises in a face-centred unit cell. What is the length of a side of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic radius \(r = 0.144\text{ nm}\); lattice type = face-centred cubic (fcc).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Spheres touch along the face diagonal of the fcc cube.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For an fcc unit cell, \(a = 2\sqrt{2}r\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a = 2 \times 1.414 \times 0.144\text{ nm} = 2.828 \times 0.144\text{ nm} = 0.407\text{ nm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(a > 2r = 0.288\text{ nm}\), the value is physically consistent. The edge length of the gold unit cell is \(0.407\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q40 - Number of unit cells in 1.00 cm3 of aluminium

questiontext.text: Aluminium crystallises in a cubic close-packed (ccp) structure with a metallic radius of \(125\text{ pm}\). How many unit cells are present in \(1.00\text{ cm}^3\) of aluminium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Lattice = ccp (fcc); metallic radius \(r = 125\text{ pm} = 125 \times 10^{-10}\text{ cm}\); total volume \(V_{\text{total}} = 1.00\text{ cm}^3\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All unit cells fill space without gaps.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For ccp, \(a = 2\sqrt{2}r\); volume of one unit cell \(= a^3\); number of unit cells \(= \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{a^3}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Edge length \(a = 2\sqrt{2} \times 125\text{ pm} = 2 \times 1.414 \times 125\text{ pm} = 353.5\text{ pm} = 3.535 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\).
Volume of one unit cell \(= (3.535 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = 4.42 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3\).
Number of unit cells in \(1.00\text{ cm}^3 = \frac{1.00}{4.42 \times 10^{-23}} = 2.26 \times 10^{22}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The order of magnitude \(10^{22}\) unit cells per \(\text{cm}^3\) is typical for metals. There are \(2.26 \times 10^{22}\) unit cells in \(1.00\text{ cm}^3\) of aluminium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q41 - Ratio of atomic radii for same edge length in sc, bcc, fcc

questiontext.text: If simple cubic (sc), body-centred cubic (bcc), and face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cells all have the same edge length \(a\), what is the ratio of the atomic radii \(r_{\text{sc}} : r_{\text{bcc}} : r_{\text{fcc}}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Edge length \(a\) is identical for sc, bcc, and fcc unit cells.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Atoms are hard spheres touching along the edge (sc), body diagonal (bcc), or face diagonal (fcc).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(r_{\text{sc}} = \frac{a}{2}\); \(r_{\text{bcc}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}a}{4}\); \(r_{\text{fcc}} = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[r_{\text{sc}} : r_{\text{bcc}} : r_{\text{fcc}} = \frac{a}{2} : \frac{\sqrt{3}a}{4} : \frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}\]
Dividing by \(a\) gives \(\frac{1}{2} : \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} : \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Numerically, \(0.500 : 0.433 : 0.354\), so \(r_{\text{sc}} > r_{\text{bcc}} > r_{\text{fcc}}\), confirming \(\frac{1}{2} : \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} : \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q42 - Density of silver ccp crystal

questiontext.text: Silver (atomic mass \(= 107.9\text{ u}\)) forms a ccp lattice with a unit cell edge length of \(408.6\text{ pm}\). What is the density of silver? (\(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Lattice = ccp (\(z = 4\)); \(M = 107.9\text{ g mol}^{-1}\); \(a = 408.6\text{ pm} = 4.086 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\); \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Unit cell density equals the bulk density of silver.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(d = \frac{z M}{a^3 N_A}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a^3 = (4.086 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = 6.822 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3\]
\[d = \frac{4 \times 107.9}{(6.822 \times 10^{-23}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23})} = \frac{431.6}{41.08} \approx 10.5\text{ g cm}^{-3}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units simplify to \(\text{g cm}^{-3}\), and \(10.5\text{ g cm}^{-3}\) matches the known density of silver.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q43 - Atomic mass of copper from fcc unit cell

questiontext.text: Copper crystallises in an fcc unit cell with an edge length of \(3.608 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\) and a density of \(8.92\text{ g cm}^{-3}\). What is the atomic mass of copper? (\(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Lattice = fcc (\(z = 4\)); \(a = 3.608 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\); \(d = 8.92\text{ g cm}^{-3}\); \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All unit cells are identical and defect-free.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(M = \frac{d N_A a^3}{z}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a^3 = (3.608 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = 4.697 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3\]
\[M = \frac{8.92 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 4.697 \times 10^{-23}}{4} = \frac{252.3}{4} \approx 63.1\text{ g mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The atomic mass of copper is \(63.1\text{ u}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q44 - Nature of cubic unit cell from molar mass and density

questiontext.text: An element with molar mass \(2.7 \times 10^{-2}\text{ kg mol}^{-1}\) forms a cubic unit cell with edge length \(405\text{ pm}\). If its density is \(2.7 \times 10^{3}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\), what is the nature of the cubic unit cell? (\(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(M = 2.7 \times 10^{-2}\text{ kg mol}^{-1}\); \(a = 405\text{ pm} = 4.05 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\); \(d = 2.7 \times 10^{3}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
SI units are used consistently (\(\text{kg}, \text{m}, \text{mol}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(z = \frac{d a^3 N_A}{M}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a^3 = (4.05 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m})^3 = 6.643 \times 10^{-29}\text{ m}^3\]
\[z = \frac{(2.7 \times 10^{3}) \times (6.643 \times 10^{-29}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23})}{2.7 \times 10^{-2}} = 6.643 \times 6.022 \times 10^{-1} \approx 4.00\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(z = 4\) atoms per unit cell, the cubic unit cell is face-centred cubic (fcc/ccp).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q45 - Number of atoms in 208 g of bcc element

questiontext.text: An element has a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure with a cell edge of \(288\text{ pm}\) and a density of \(7.2\text{ g cm}^{-3}\). How many atoms are present in \(208\text{ g}\) of the element?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Structure = bcc (\(z = 2\)); \(a = 288\text{ pm} = 2.88 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\); \(d = 7.2\text{ g cm}^{-3}\); sample mass \(= 208\text{ g}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each bcc unit cell contains \(2\) atoms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Total volume} = \frac{\text{mass}}{d}\); \(\text{number of unit cells} = \frac{\text{total volume}}{a^3}\); \(\text{total atoms} = z \times \text{number of unit cells}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Volume of one unit cell \(= (2.88 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = 2.39 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3\).
Volume of \(208\text{ g}\) sample \(= \frac{208}{7.2} = 28.89\text{ cm}^3\).
Number of unit cells \(= \frac{28.89}{2.39 \times 10^{-23}} = 12.08 \times 10^{23}\).
Total atoms \(= 2 \times 12.08 \times 10^{23} = 24.16 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(24.16 \times 10^{23}\) atoms (or \(2.416 \times 10^{24}\) atoms) are present in \(208\text{ g}\) of the element.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q46 - Atomic radius of niobium from bcc density

questiontext.text: Niobium crystallises in a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure. If its density is \(8.55\text{ g cm}^{-3}\) and atomic mass is \(93\text{ u}\), what is the atomic radius of niobium? (\(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Structure = bcc (\(z = 2\)); \(d = 8.55\text{ g cm}^{-3}\); \(M = 93\text{ g mol}^{-1}\); \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Atoms touch along the body diagonal in bcc.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(a^3 = \frac{zM}{d N_A}\) and \(r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a^3 = \frac{2 \times 93}{8.55 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = \frac{186}{5.149 \times 10^{24}} = 3.612 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3 = 36.12 \times 10^{-24}\text{ cm}^3\]
Taking the cube root: \(a = 3.306 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm} = 330.6\text{ pm}\).
Atomic radius \(r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 330.6\text{ pm} = \frac{1.732 \times 330.6}{4} \approx 143.1\text{ pm}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The calculated atomic radius of niobium is \(143.1\text{ pm}\) (or \(0.143\text{ nm}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q47 - Percentage of Schottky defects in NaCl at room temperature

questiontext.text: In \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) at room temperature, there are approximately \(10^{6}\) Schottky pairs per \(\text{cm}^3\) and about \(10^{22}\) ions per \(\text{cm}^3\). Roughly how many ions correspond to one Schottky defect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of Schottky pairs per \(\text{cm}^3 = 10^{6}\); total number of ions per \(\text{cm}^3 = 10^{22}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Schottky defects are distributed uniformly throughout the crystal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Ions per Schottky defect} = \frac{\text{Total ions per cm}^3}{\text{Schottky pairs per cm}^3}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\text{Ions per Schottky defect} = \frac{10^{22}}{10^{6}} = 10^{16}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
There is approximately one Schottky defect per \(10^{16}\) ions in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) at room temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q48 - Mass of one unit cell from density and edge length

questiontext.text: A cubic crystal has an edge length of \(3.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\) and a density of \(5.0\text{ g cm}^{-3}\). What is the mass of a single unit cell of this crystal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Edge length \(a = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}\); density \(d = 5.0\text{ g cm}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Unit cell density equals bulk density.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Mass of unit cell} = d \times V = d \times a^3\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a^3 = (3.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = 2.7 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3\]
\[\text{Mass of unit cell} = 5.0\text{ g cm}^{-3} \times 2.7 \times 10^{-23}\text{ cm}^3 = 1.35 \times 10^{-22}\text{ g}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The mass of one unit cell is \(1.35 \times 10^{-22}\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q49 - Effect of vacancy defect on density

questiontext.text: Which type of defect can arise when a non-ionic solid is heated, and how does it affect the density of the solid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heating a crystalline solid increases thermal vibration and can cause atoms or molecules to leave their normal lattice sites.

Step 2: Evaluation
When some lattice sites become vacant upon heating, a vacancy defect develops. Since the mass of the crystal decreases while its volume remains essentially unchanged, the density of the solid decreases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A vacancy defect arises upon heating, and it decreases the density of the solid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q50 - Stoichiometric defects in ZnS and AgBr

questiontext.text: Which stoichiometric defect(s) are shown by \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{AgBr}\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frenkel defect occurs in ionic solids with a large size difference between cations and anions, whereas Schottky defect occurs when cations and anions are of similar sizes.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{ZnS}\) shows Frenkel defect due to the small size of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions. \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) is a special ionic solid that shows both Frenkel and Schottky defects.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{ZnS}\) shows Frenkel defect, and \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) shows both Frenkel and Schottky defects.

Both Frenkel and Schottky in \(\mathrm{ZnS}\); Schottky only in \(\mathrm{AgBr}\)
Frenkel defect in \(\mathrm{ZnS}\); Schottky defect only in \(\mathrm{AgBr}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q51 - Why ZnO turns yellow on heating

questiontext.text: Zinc oxide (\(\mathrm{ZnO}\)) is white at room temperature, but on heating it turns yellow and forms \(\mathrm{Zn}_{1+x}\mathrm{O}\). This happens because of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heating \(\mathrm{ZnO}\) causes reversible loss of oxygen and creates a metal excess defect.

Step 2: Evaluation
Upon heating, \(\mathrm{ZnO} \to \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^-\). The excess \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions move into interstitial sites, and the released electrons move into neighbouring interstitial sites, imparting a yellow colour.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{ZnO}\) turns yellow on heating due to a metal excess defect caused by extra \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions and electrons at interstitial sites.

metal deficiency defect due to missing \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q52 - Concentration of cation vacancies in SrCl2 doped NaCl

questiontext.text: If \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is doped with \(10^{-3}\text{ mol }\%\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\), what is the concentration of cation vacancies per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)? (\(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Doping level \(= 10^{-3}\text{ mol }\%\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\); \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each divalent \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion replaces two \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions to maintain electrical neutrality, occupying one site and creating \(1\) cation vacancy.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Cation vacancies per mol } \mathrm{NaCl} = \text{moles of } \mathrm{SrCl}_2 \text{ per mol } \mathrm{NaCl} \times N_A\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(10^{-3}\text{ mol }\%\) means \(100\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) contains \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\).
Therefore, \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) contains \(\frac{10^{-3}}{100} = 10^{-5}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ions.
Number of cation vacancies per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl} = 10^{-5} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{18}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The concentration of cation vacancies is \(6.022 \times 10^{18}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q53 - Fractions of Ni2+ and Ni3+ in Ni0.98O1.00

questiontext.text: Analysis shows that nickel oxide has the formula \(\mathrm{Ni}_{0.98}\mathrm{O}_{1.00}\). What percentage of nickel ions exist as \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Formula is \(\mathrm{Ni}_{0.98}\mathrm{O}_{1.00}\), meaning \(98\) nickel ions per \(100\) oxide (\(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\)) ions.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the number of \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\) ions be \(x\) and \(\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}\) ions be \(98 - x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By electrical neutrality, total positive charge equals total negative charge.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Total negative charge on \(100\ \mathrm{O}^{2-}\) ions \(= 200\).
\[2x + 3(98 - x) = 200\]
\[2x + 294 - 3x = 200 \implies x = 94\]
So, \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+} = 94\) and \(\mathrm{Ni}^{3+} = 98 - 94 = 4\).
Percentage of \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+} = \frac{94}{98} \times 100\% \approx 95.9\% \approx 96\%\).
Percentage of \(\mathrm{Ni}^{3+} = \frac{4}{98} \times 100\% \approx 4.1\% \approx 4\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(96\% + 4\% = 100\%\), and \(94(+2) + 4(+3) = 188 + 12 = 200\). Thus, \(96\%\) exist as \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\) and \(4\%\) as \(\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q54 - F centres in alkali halides

questiontext.text: What are F-centres in alkali halide crystals such as \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) heated in sodium vapour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
F-centres (from German *Farbenzenter*, meaning colour centre) are responsible for the colour developed in metal-excess alkali halides.

Step 2: Evaluation
When \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is heated in sodium vapour, \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions diffuse to the surface and electrons released by \(\mathrm{Na}\) atoms diffuse into the crystal to occupy the vacant anionic sites. These anionic sites occupied by unpaired electrons are called F-centres.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
F-centres are anionic vacancies occupied by unpaired electrons.

Equal numbers of missing cations and anions

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q55 - Band theory distinction between conductors, semiconductors, insulators

questiontext.text: In terms of band theory, how does an insulator differ from a semiconductor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In solids, atomic orbitals form closely spaced energy bands: a filled valence band and a higher-energy unoccupied conduction band.

Step 2: Evaluation
In an insulator, the energy gap (forbidden zone) between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band is very large, so electrons cannot jump across it. In a semiconductor, this energy gap is small, allowing some electrons to jump to the conduction band, especially as temperature rises.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An insulator has a large energy gap between the valence band and conduction band, whereas a semiconductor has a small energy gap.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q56 - Doping group 14 element to form n type semiconductor

questiontext.text: To convert a group \(14\) element like silicon into an \(n\)-type semiconductor, it should be doped with an element belonging to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An \(n\)-type semiconductor has excess negatively charged delocalised electrons introduced by an electron-rich impurity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Group \(14\) elements have \(4\) valence electrons. Doping with a group \(15\) element (such as \(\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{As}\)) having \(5\) valence electrons uses \(4\) electrons for covalent bonding and leaves the \(5\)th electron extra and delocalised, producing an \(n\)-type semiconductor.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The impurity should belong to group \(15\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q57 - Why non stoichiometric Cu2O is a p type semiconductor

questiontext.text: Non-stoichiometric cuprous oxide (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{O}\)) prepared in the laboratory has a copper-to-oxygen ratio slightly less than \(2:1\). Why does this substance behave as a \(p\)-type semiconductor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A copper-to-oxygen ratio slightly less than \(2:1\) indicates a metal deficiency defect where some \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions are missing.

Step 2: Evaluation
To maintain electrical neutrality when \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions are missing, some remaining \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions are oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions. The presence of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions creates positive holes in the lattice, enabling conduction via positive holes (\(p\)-type semiconductor).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Some \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions are replaced by \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, creating positive holes that make it a \(p\)-type semiconductor.

answer.text: Extra \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions occupy interstitial sites and release free electrons.
Some \(\mathrm{Cu}^+\) ions are missing and charge is balanced by \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, creating positive holes.
Oxygen vacancies trap unpaired electrons forming F-centres.
Copper atoms form metallic domains with overlapping bands.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q58 - Group 13-15 and 12-16 compound semiconductors

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets contains only group \(13\text{–}15\) compound semiconductors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Compound semiconductors formed from group \(13\) (\(\mathrm{Al, Ga, In}\)) and group \(15\) (\(\mathrm{P, As, Sb}\)) elements simulate an average valence of four, like \(\mathrm{Si}\) and \(\mathrm{Ge}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{InSb}\), \(\mathrm{AlP}\), and \(\mathrm{GaAs}\) are group \(13\text{–}15\) compounds, whereas \(\mathrm{ZnS}\), \(\mathrm{CdS}\), \(\mathrm{CdSe}\), and \(\mathrm{HgTe}\) are group \(12\text{–}16\) compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{InSb}\), \(\mathrm{AlP}\), and \(\mathrm{GaAs}\) are all group \(13\text{–}15\) compound semiconductors.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q59 - Origin and unit of magnetic moment

questiontext.text: The magnetic moment of an electron in an atom originates from its orbital motion around the nucleus and its spin around its own axis. What is the value of one Bohr magneton (\(\mu_B\))?

generalfeedback.text:

The magnetic moment of a single electron is extremely small and is expressed in Bohr magnetons (\(\mu_B\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
One Bohr magneton is equal to \(9.27 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The value of \(1\ \mu_B\) is \(9.27 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q60 - Domain alignment in ferrimagnetism and effect of heating

questiontext.text: Which statement is correct regarding ferrimagnetic substances such as \(\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{O}_4\) and \(\mathrm{MgFe}_2\mathrm{O}_4\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ferrimagnetism arises when magnetic moments of domains in a solid are aligned in parallel and anti-parallel directions in unequal numbers.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because of unequal parallel and anti-parallel alignments, ferrimagnetic substances possess a net magnetic moment and are weakly attracted by a magnetic field compared to ferromagnetic substances. On heating, thermal agitation randomises the domain alignment, causing them to lose ferrimagnetism and become paramagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ferrimagnetic substances have unequal parallel and anti-parallel domain alignments and become paramagnetic on heating.

answer.text: Their domains are aligned in equal opposite directions, giving zero net magnetic moment.
They are strongly repelled by an external magnetic field.
Their domains are aligned in parallel and anti-parallel directions in unequal numbers, and they become paramagnetic on heating.
They retain permanent magnetisation even at extremely high temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q61 - Why ferromagnetic substances make better permanent magnets

questiontext.text: Why do ferromagnetic substances make better permanent magnets than ferrimagnetic substances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Permanent magnets require strong net magnetic moment and persistent alignment of magnetic domains after the external field is removed.

Step 2: Evaluation
In ferromagnetic substances (such as \(\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Co}, \mathrm{Ni}, \mathrm{Gd}, \mathrm{CrO}_2\)), all domains align parallel to the applied magnetic field, producing a very strong magnetic effect, and this ordering persists even after the external field is removed. In ferrimagnetic substances, some domains oppose others, resulting in a much weaker net magnetic moment.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ferromagnetic substances make better permanent magnets because all their domains align in the same direction and retain that alignment after the magnetic field is removed.

answer.text: Ferromagnetic substances have all electrons paired, preventing demagnetisation.
Ferrimagnetic substances have zero domain structure in the solid state.
Ferromagnetic substances are weakly repelled by magnetic fields, stabilising their domains.
In ferromagnetic substances, all domains align in the direction of the magnetic field and this ordering persists even when the field is removed.
